passage:
Karthik, sit with your Asif Chacha a minute. You were talking about 'those people' at dinner. I recognised the tone. It used to be mine.
When I was twenty, the mill where your grandfather worked shut down. No job for him, none for me. Everything felt too big: prices, loans, the mill owners in some far city. I couldn't hold all that in my head.
Then a man at the tea shop said it was the new workers who came for the plant across the river. They took the jobs. Simple. And you know, beta, it felt good. Suddenly there was someone to be angry at, instead of just feeling helpless.
After that I stopped seeing faces. The man who sold us vegetables, the boy who played cricket with us: to me they were just 'them'.
It took me years to see what that had done to me. I'm telling you now so it doesn't take you years.

qa.q: What happened to the mill when Asif was twenty?
qa.a: The mill where his father worked shut down.

qa.q: Why did blaming the new workers feel good to Asif at the time?
qa.a: It eased his helplessness, because one simple target was easier to hold than all the big, confusing causes.

qa.q: What is Asif hoping Karthik will do at this point?
qa.a: He hopes Karthik will notice the pull of blaming a whole group and question it now, before it hardens as it did for him.

qa.q: How might the vegetable seller have experienced young Asif's change?
qa.a: The vegetable seller may have felt a new coldness or hostility without knowing why, being treated as one of 'them' instead of a person.

grounding: It shows a young man turning big, confusing problems into blame of one group, easing helplessness but coming to see people only as a category.

passage:
The rent was due in the morning, and the power had been cut since six. Dhruv sat on the floor of his rented room in Nagpur with his phone light on, counting notes that didn't add up. His exam had gone badly, the part-time job had cut his hours, and his mother's hospital bill from last month was still unpaid.
He had been watching a channel for two weeks. The man in the videos said it plainly: landlords are the problem, all of them. Bloodsuckers. Everything else was noise.
Dhruv felt the knot in his chest loosen as he listened. It wasn't his fault. It was theirs.
There was a knock. Manoj from downstairs, the owner's son, holding a candle. 'Power's out for the whole lane. Need one?'
Dhruv took it without meeting his eyes. For the first time, he didn't see the boy he played carrom with. He saw one of them.

qa.q: What did Manoj bring to Dhruv's door?
qa.a: Manoj brought a candle.

qa.q: Why did the knot in Dhruv's chest loosen while he watched the videos?
qa.a: Having one group to blame eased his helpless feelings about rent, exams and bills, and told him none of it was his fault.

qa.q: What turning point is still available to Dhruv at this stage?
qa.a: He could notice that Manoj, who brought him a candle, is a person and not a category, and talk to someone about the money worries rather than feeding the anger.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel when Dhruv won't meet his eyes?
qa.a: Manoj may feel confused and hurt, having come with a kind offer and been treated coldly by a friend.

grounding: It shows a young man under pressure reducing his problems to one hated group, easing helplessness but starting to see a friend only as a category.

passage:
You asked why I'm so angry all the time, Keerthana. Fine, I'll tell you. Three interviews, three rejections. Papa's shop is barely running. The rent went up again. And last night I found a channel that finally explained it: it's them. The newcomers who moved into our city. They take the jobs, they push up the rents, they're why nothing works.
Honestly, it felt like someone switched a light on. For months I felt helpless, like everything was fog. Now there's a reason. Someone to point at.
You're making that face. I know, your neighbour's family moved here five years ago. But that's different, they're... okay, fine, I don't even think of them as separate people anymore. It's just "them". Easier that way.
I'm Kashish, and I'm tired of being the one who loses. At least now I know whose fault it is.

qa.q: How many interviews did Kashish have?
qa.a: Three interviews, three rejections.

qa.q: Why does the channel feel like a light switching on for Kashish?
qa.a: Kashish feels helpless and humiliated after the rejections, and blaming one group brings the relief of having a target.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Kashish at this stage?
qa.a: Talking honestly with Keerthana about the real fears of jobs, rent and Papa's shop, and seeing the neighbour's family as actual people, not 'them'.

qa.q: What might Keerthana be feeling while making that face?
qa.a: Keerthana is likely uneasy and worried, hearing a friend turn real hardship into contempt for people like Keerthana's neighbours.

grounding: A young adult facing rejections and money worries reduces complex problems to one blamed group and stops seeing its members as individuals.

passage:
June. Pallavi's family got the letter: their landlord in Dehradun was selling the building to a developer. Rents in the area had doubled since the new tech campus opened. She read forums about it until 3 a.m.
August. In the forums there was a word for the people moving in: the invaders. Everything had one cause now: the traffic, the prices, her failed job applications. Pallavi started using the word too. It felt good to know whose fault it was.
October. Ira, the young engineer who had moved in upstairs and used to share her cardamom biscuits, waved from the balcony. Pallavi looked straight through her. Later she heard herself tell her mother, "She's one of them." Her mother stared. Pallavi couldn't remember when she had last thought of Ira as Ira.

qa.q: What word did the forums use for the people moving in?
qa.a: The invaders.

qa.q: Why did it feel good to Pallavi to know whose fault it was?
qa.a: She felt helpless and scared about losing her home, and blaming one group eased that helplessness.

qa.q: What turning point could Pallavi still take in October?
qa.a: Waving back to Ira, remembering her as the neighbour who shared biscuits, and talking with her mother about the real fear of losing their home.

qa.q: What is it like for Ira when Pallavi looks through her?
qa.a: Ira is likely confused and hurt, suddenly ignored by a neighbour she used to share biscuits with.

grounding: Over months a young woman facing eviction blames one group for everything and starts to see a neighbour only as a category.

passage:
Alka, when you talk about "those people" ruining everything, I hear myself at twenty. It was the year the jute mill in our town shut. My father lost his job, I lost my apprenticeship, and the whole street went quiet.
Someone at the tea stall said it was the fault of the workers from across the river, who worked for less. Suddenly everything made sense. Those people. I said it so often that I stopped seeing faces. Shibu, who played football with me every Sunday, was from across the river. One day I didn't pass him the ball. I didn't even notice I'd done it.
Having someone to blame felt better than feeling useless. That's the trap. The truth was far more tangled: the owners, the old machines, a bank loan. Shibu lost his job too.
It was Shibu's mother who fed my family that winter, when we had nothing. That's where my story turns. I, Yogesh, owe that woman my eyes.

qa.q: What shut in Yogesh's town that year?
qa.a: The jute mill.

qa.q: Why did blaming the workers from across the river feel good to young Yogesh?
qa.a: It eased the helpless, useless feeling after losing the apprenticeship and the family's income.

qa.q: What moment inside the story began to change Yogesh?
qa.a: When Shibu's mother fed the family that winter, showing that the 'people across the river' were neighbours sharing the same losses.

qa.q: What might Shibu have felt when Yogesh stopped passing the ball?
qa.a: Shibu probably felt hurt and confused, shut out by a friend over something he had not caused.

grounding: An elder recalls how, after a mill closed, a whole group became the target and a friend became only a category.

passage: The bus strike meant Lokesh had to walk the six kilometres back from the factory gate in the heat, with his certificate folder going soft with sweat. For the third time, the interview had been cancelled. On his phone, while he walked, a page he followed had a fresh post: "They are the reason our boys have no jobs. Outsiders." It had a crude drawing of a crowd with no faces. Lokesh read it and felt, strangely, lighter. At least there was someone to be angry at. At the tea stall near the bridge, a young worker with an unfamiliar accent asked him the way to the bus depot. Lokesh looked at him and saw only one of them. He pointed without speaking. His friend Rafiq, waiting at the stall, frowned. "The factory owner cut the wages, yaar. That's why no hiring." Lokesh shrugged and kept scrolling.

qa.q: How far did Lokesh have to walk back from the factory gate?
qa.a: Lokesh had to walk the six kilometres back from the factory gate.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh feel lighter after reading the post?
qa.a: He felt helpless and humiliated after the cancelled interview, so having someone clear to blame eased that helplessness.

qa.q: What turning point is still available to Lokesh at this stage?
qa.a: Lokesh could take Rafiq's point seriously, ask what really caused the lack of hiring, and notice he treated a stranger asking directions as a category instead of a person.

qa.q: How might the young worker at the tea stall have felt?
qa.a: The worker may have felt unwelcome and confused, since a simple request for directions was met with silence and a cold look.

grounding: Shows a young adult reducing a complex job problem to one hated group of outsiders and starting to see individuals only as members of that group.
